Software archaeology · Commodore 64 · 1984

A photograph of somebody’s desk

Jeff Minter’s Revenge of the Mutant Camels shipped with his own source code still lying about inside it, a spare copy of his sprites, half a tune he had already used, a cheat that does almost nothing, and a payphone.

Revenge of the Mutant Camels · Llamasoft, 1984 47,390 bytes · $0801–$C11E

A 1984 Commodore 64 game is a strange kind of document. It is a program, obviously. But it is also the only surviving record of a working session: a snapshot of what one person happened to have in memory on the afternoon they decided it was done. Revenge of the Mutant Camels is a very good example, because the person in question was Jeff Minter, who worked fast, wrote his own tools, and did not tidy up.

The game is easy to describe. You are a camel. You walk to the right through forty-two scrolling landscapes, shooting things, while things shoot back. The things are kangaroos, telephone kiosks, helicopters, parachutists, llamas and Pac-Man. That was enough.

What follows is what falls out of the file when you take it apart: the table holding those forty-two zones, the font that had to have an apostrophe added so a joke would work, the tune that is in there twice, the cheat code that is a lie, and the reason the random numbers are Microsoft BASIC.

How we got at it

The disk holds a crunched file. Loading it gives you a two-line BASIC stub and a decruncher, and reading that statically stops after a few dozen instructions — everything interesting is produced at run time. So the program was run: 1,768,854 instructions, 287 video frames, ending the moment the loader called the KERNAL to fetch the next file. The memory at that instant — 47,390 bytes from $0801 to $C11E — is what everything below is read out of.

Every address in this piece is an address in that image. The screenshots come from booting it on an emulated 6510 with real BASIC and KERNAL ROMs banked in, which matters more than it sounds. See the section on random numbers.

Forty-two zones, and their names

The box said forty-two attack waves, and so, in his own words at $5AB6, does the author: “THE GAME CONSISTS OF FORTY TWO DIFFERENT ATTACK WAVES.” The code agrees, which is less common than you would hope.

At $6700 there is a table of exactly forty-two records of exactly two hundred bytes each, running to $87CF — 8,400 bytes, a fifth of the entire program. Each record is one zone. At offset $A0 inside it sits a forty-byte field, exactly one line of a Commodore 64 screen, holding the zone’s name already centred by hand with spaces.

Here they all are, as the program stores them.

    One is Pink Floyd. One lists Pac-Man’s ghosts and gets the fourth deliberately wrong — INKY, PINKY, BLINKY, AND THUD! One is about the Sinclair Spectrum’s rubber keyboard. Three are puns on ewe. Zone 5 is Attack of the Mutant Mutant Camels — the title of the prequel with an extra mutant in it — and zone 42 is Revenge of the Mutant Mutant Camels, which is what happens when a game’s title is already a sequel to a joke.

    How we know — the table is 42 × 200

    Three independent routes agree.

    From the code. The routine that steps from one zone to the next, at $93E4, does LDA $3E / CLC / ADC #$C8 / STA $3E — add two hundred to the zone pointer — starting from $6700, loaded as $67/$00 at $93D3 and $93DE.

    From the bytes. Scanning the image for forty-byte runs of printable text finds them at $67A0 and then every 200 bytes after it, forty-two times, ending at $87A8. Nothing else in the image matches that stride.

    From the author’s own source, which is still in the file. See the last section: one of the surviving fragments is the loop that steps the table, and it reads CLC / ADC #$C8 / STA NEXINI.

    The names are stored as screen codes, not ASCII — $01 is A — which is why an ordinary string search misses them, and why the punctuation is where it is.

    A zone is a graph, and an explosion is a creature

    The other 160 bytes of each record are the interesting part, and they are not laid out the way you would guess. A zone defines eight creature types, and you might expect eight little structures side by side. Instead the record is stored the other way round: nineteen fields, each one an array of eight bytes, one per type. All eight lifetimes together, then all eight sprite ranges together. Column-major — which is exactly the shape you get if you are hand-assembling a table and want to type each row of numbers on one line.

    OffsetField (×8, one byte per creature type)
    +$10, +$18first and last sprite frame — the animation range
    +$38nextType — what this creature turns into. $FF means gone for good.
    +$80lifetime, in ticks. Zero means the countdown never fires.
    +$98…+$9Feight per-zone settings
    +$A0the forty-character name

    The field that makes the game is +$38. Every live creature has a countdown; when it reaches zero, a routine at $9A39 looks up that creature’s nextType and — unless it is $FF — jumps straight into the spawn routine at $9772 with the same slot and the new type. The creature does not die. It becomes something else, in place.

    Take zone 10, Telecom’s Comeuppance. British Telecom was privatised in November 1984. Here is what its record says, drawn from its own sprite pointers:

    Now look at the last link in that chain. In thirty-nine of the forty-two zones there is exactly one creature type whose sprite range is $EC–$EE, whose lifetime is twelve, and whose nextType is $FF. The same three frames, in nearly every zone, whatever the theme.

    There is no explosion subsystem in this game. There is no kill routine and no particle code. When you shoot something, the thing you shot is turned into the explosion creature, which lives for twelve ticks and then, being the one type allowed to reach $FF, is allowed to go away. Blowing something up and a bird laying an egg are the same call.

    How we know — the transformation, and the three zones that are different

    $9A39 is the per-frame countdown. It decrements this slot’s timer; at zero it loads the slot’s own type, reloads the lifetime from the zone template at +$80, then reads +$38 — nextType. CMP #$FF: equal, and it jumps to $9328, which frees the slot for good. Otherwise TAY and JMP $9772, the spawn routine, with the same slot index still in X.

    The field offsets were traced from the two live routines that use them and then checked against the raw bytes of five different zones. Reading the whole nextType column across all forty-two turns up three exceptions, and all three look deliberate:

    Zone 4, Wacky Whackers, has its own explosion — sprite $A8, sixteen ticks instead of twelve. Its four chained types all share the identical sprite range $A3–$A7 with different lifetimes, so the same picture behaves four different ways.

    Zone 7 has two explosions, $EC–$ED at two ticks and $EC–$EE at six.

    Zone 11, Have A Go At These…, has no type with nextType = $FF at all. Nothing in that zone is ever allowed to disappear on its own.

    The zone whose creatures come back

    Reading the nextType column across all forty-two zones gives you forty-two little directed graphs, and most of them are short chains like the payphone. Eleven contain a two-step loop — A becomes B becomes A — which is really just a slow animation done with the transformation machinery.

    Exactly one zone has a longer cycle. Zone 7: type 0 becomes type 2 becomes type 3 becomes type 4 becomes type 0, with lifetimes of 106, 13, 106 and 13 ticks. And there are only two sprites involved, because $9A and $9B are the same creature mirrored.

    Zone 7 is called HAVEN’T WE MET SOMEWHERE BEFORE?

    The eight settings, and the one that is read and thrown away

    Eight bytes at +$98 carry the per-zone knobs, and a routine at $9CB5 loads them in order at the start of every wave. Two go straight into the video chip’s sprite-colour registers, so every zone has its own two-colour palette baked into the table. One, at +$9B, is the cap on how many creatures may be alive at once: it is 8 in forty-one zones and 6 in exactly one — zone 7, the one with the loop. Somebody found that zone too crowded and turned it down by two. One, at +$9C, ramps with the zone number in four flat steps — zero for zones 1 to 26, then 2, then 4, then 6 for the last six — a difficulty tier declared in blocks rather than tuned smoothly.

    The first three are the interesting ones, and they are what makes the picture at the top of this page look the way it does. Each is a bitmask over the eight creature types, and when a creature is spawned its bit is ORed into one of three video-chip registers:

    ByteWhat its bits switch on, per creature type
    +$98multicolour — half the horizontal resolution, two extra colours
    +$99double height
    +$9Adouble width

    So the look of a creature is not a property of its picture. It is a property of the zone it turns up in — and fifteen of the game’s sprite ranges are rendered differently in different waves. Sprite $30 is a plain single-colour thing in Careful With That Axe, Eugene and a multicolour one in Fast Food Is Bad For Camels. Best of all, the three-frame range $2D–$2F is used by two different creature types inside the same zone — Zapstars III: Geometrica — one of them double width and one of them not. Same pixels, twice, on the same screen, at two different sizes.

    Zone 1’s +$9A is $63 — bits 0, 1, 5 and 6 — and creature types 0, 1, 5 and 6 of zone 1 are the birds. That is why the birds in the photograph are twice as wide as the picture stored for them. The camel is a separate case and is expanded in both axes in every zone, by two instructions in the same loader that owe nothing to the data: LDA #$01 / STA $D017 / STA $D01D. Sprite zero is the player, always, everywhere, at four times its stored area.

    And then there is +$9F, which is zero in all forty-two zones. It is not merely unused. The loader fetches it — the eighth call in a run of eight — and then, before the value can be stored anywhere, loads #$01 over the top of it on the very next instruction:

    9CDA  20 FB 9C   JSR $9CFB      ; fetch the eighth byte…
9CDD  A9 01      LDA #$01       ; …and immediately lose it
9CDF  8D 17 D0   STA $D017
9CE2  8D 1D D0   STA $D01D

    Somebody laid out a record with a field in it, wrote the code to read the field, and then never wrote the code to use it. Forty-two zeroes, read once a wave since 1984, and dropped every time.

    A font with jokes in it

    The game does not use the Commodore character set. At $2000 it keeps its own — 128 glyphs, installed by a single write of #$18 to $D018 at $8AE7. Here it is, whole.

    Six consecutive codes, in an order that matches no standard on the machine — not ASCII, not PETSCII, not the screen codes the rest of the text uses. The positions where a Commodore would keep those marks are occupied here by digits and by landscape tiles. So six glyphs were drawn and dropped into a gap, because the zone names needed them: you cannot write HAVEN’T WE MET SOMEWHERE BEFORE? without an apostrophe and a question mark.

    You can watch it work. In the screenshot of zone one further up, the two bytes $54 $54 at the end of the stored name come out on a real screen as !!.

    There is a second half to this, and it explains something you have already looked at without noticing. Most text in the game is stored in ordinary ASCII and masked with AND #$3F on its way to the screen, which folds the letters down into the low sixty-four codes. That leaves the upper half of the font unreachable by ordinary text — a second bank of glyphs at code plus $40, which nothing can print by accident.

    Then there is the status bar. The routine at $9091 draws the line reading NEUTRONIUM STATUS followed by a row of Hs, and it masks every byte it copies except when the byte is literally an ASCII H — one CMP #$48 and a branch, for that character alone. Masked, H is the letter. Unmasked, code $48 is a solid bar.

    The credits are made of ground

    There is no routine in this program that draws the credits. No scrolling-message subsystem, no text buffer, nothing you could point at and call a title sequence.

    What there is instead: the landscape scrolls right to left, and every time a new column of terrain arrives at the right-hand edge, the routine that builds it also plants one character of the credit text and one character of the high-score table into that column. The words are terrain. They arrive at the speed the ground arrives, because they are the ground.

    How we know — one character per column

    The routine is at $56EC, and it runs once a frame. It fills a seven-byte buffer at $1FF0 with spaces — that buffer is the next column of terrain — and then writes exactly two characters into it:

    5704  A6 5B      LDX $5B
5706  BD 00 5E   LDA $5E00,X   ; one byte of the high-score table
5709  8D F3 1F   STA $1FF3     ; → row 3 of the new column
570C  8A         TXA
570D  A8         TAY
570E  B1 5C      LDA ($5C),Y   ; one byte of the credit text
5710  8D F5 1F   STA $1FF5     ; → row 5 of the new column
5713  C0 FF      CPY #$FF
5715  D0 0C      BNE $5723
5717  E6 5D      INC $5D       ; next page of credits
...
5723  E6 5B      INC $5B       ; and step both, one character

    $5C/$5D is the credit pointer, and it is set to $5A00 — the start of the credit text — during start-up at $8A96. When it reaches $5E the whole thing has been read out and the attract mode resets.

    The credits themselves are the closest thing the file has to a diary entry:

    THIS PROGRAM WAS WRITTEN OVER A TWO MONTH PERIOD BY JEFF MINTER … THANKS ALSO TO WHOEVER INVENTED THE SPRITE … ESPECIAL THANKS TO THE DOG FOR NOT CHEWING UP MY FLOPPY DISKS … AND THANKS TO YOU READING THIS FOR BUYING MY GAME. UNLESS YOU COPIED IT, IN WHICH CASE MAY THE FLEAS OF 1000 CAMELS INFEST YOUR ARMPITS FOREVER.

    The menagerie

    The sprites are where the game keeps its personality, and hardly any of them are camels. They live in the first sixteen kilobytes of memory — the only place the video chip can see sprite data — and they can be pulled straight out and drawn.

    The sixteen-ton weight is at $2740, with the words 16 TONS lettered onto a shape twenty-one pixels high — a Monty Python joke, drawn a pixel at a time, in 1984.

    The jokes are in the data

    Sprite numbers appear in the zone records, so you can ask which zone uses which picture, and the answers are better than the pictures.

    The sixteen-ton weight is creature type 4 of zone 1. It is in the very first wave of the game, and its lifetime is zero, which means its clock never runs out: whatever it does, it does not go away on its own. It is the thing falling out of the sky in the picture at the top of this page — which is not a coincidence, because that picture is zone 1 and the weight was still in flight when the frame was taken.

    The peace symbol is used by zone 6. Zone 6 is called THIS KIOSK IS A NUCLEAR FREE ZONE, and four of its eight creature types are that one sprite.

    And zone 12 is called INKY, PINKY, BLINKY, AND THUD!

    The title flickers, and it is one instruction

    A multicolour sprite gets three colours: one of its own, and two shared with every other multicolour sprite on the screen. The REVENGE letters use only the two shared ones — the sprite’s own colour never appears in the data at all. One of the two is set once, to yellow, and never touched again. The other is $D025, and it is where this gets good.

    And the title screen’s main loop is eight instructions. One of them is this:

    8F7C  20 B0 8F   JSR $8FB0      ; the starfield
8F7F  EE 25 D0   INC $D025      ; ← the shared sprite colour. Just: add one.
8F82  20 70 91   JSR $9170      ; the music
8F85  20 EE 52   JSR $52EE      ; the scroll
8F88  AD 00 DC   LDA $DC00      ; fire pressed?
8F8B  29 10      AND #$10
8F8D  F0 03      BEQ $8F92      ; …then start the game
8F8F  4C 7C 8F   JMP $8F7C

    Half of every letter is a colour register being incremented in a loop. Here are six consecutive frames:

    It reads as a raster effect — a bar sweeping down the letters — because the pixels that change happen to be arranged as horizontal streaks, and because the loop is not synchronised to the video. It runs as fast as it runs, so the register advances by an unpredictable amount between one frame and the next and the colour jumps rather than sliding. A real raster bar costs you an interrupt per scanline and a table of colours. This costs three bytes and it is in the title loop next to the joystick read.

    How we know — to the pixel

    The four sprites at $34C0–$3580 contain, between them, 138 bit-pairs of value 11, 77 of value 01, and none of value 10 — so the sprite’s own colour register is never used and the letters are two-tone by construction.

    A multicolour pixel is two screen pixels wide, and the title expands these sprites in both directions ($D01D and $D017 are both set to $1F at $9056), so every bit-pair becomes eight screen pixels. 138 × 8 = 1,104. 77 × 8 = 616.

    Measured on eighteen consecutive captured frames: 1,104 pixels of yellow in every single one, and 616 pixels of a second colour that is light blue, then green, then light grey, then red, then light grey, then orange, then black, then blue, then black, then dark grey. Those are the two numbers the data predicts, and nothing in between.

    $D026 — the fixed yellow — is written twice in the whole program: once here at $9025, once per zone by the scalar loader. $D025 is written at $9020, per zone by the loader, and incremented at $8F7F. That INC is the only thing in the program that changes a colour without being told what to change it to.

    The tune you have already heard

    The music is stored as pairs of bytes: how long to hold a note, then which note. $F0 is a rest, $FF is the end. The duration is in ticks, and a tick is seven video frames — a hundred and forty milliseconds. The player runs off the raster interrupt, fifty times a second like everything else, but it counts down a divider first and only advances the music when the divider hits zero. That divider is one byte, $11. It is written once in the entire program — LDA #$07 / STA $11 at $88C2 — and read in exactly one place, by the player at $8907. The tempo of every tune in the game is that seven. The note number indexes a table of sixty-five frequencies at $898C and $89CD, and that table deserves a sentence of its own: it is true equal temperament, the octave ratio is exactly 2.0000, and it is tuned so that note zero is 31.48 Hz. Internally perfect; about a third of a semitone flat of concert pitch. Nobody would ever notice, and it is not out of tune with itself, which is the only thing that matters.

    There are three voices. All three begin with the same thirty-eight notes in unison and then split into melody, harmony and bass. It is a real three-part arrangement, and the credits say who wrote it: “THE INTRODUCTORY MUSIC WAS ARRANGED FOR THE 64 BY JAMES LISNEY.”

    The title music

    A minute and a half. This is not a reading of the data: the game was booted and left running while every write it made to the sound chip was logged with a cycle timestamp, and this is that log played back, trimmed to exactly one pass of the tune. The pitches are the values it put in the frequency registers, the durations are the gaps between the gate bits going on and off, and the envelope is the one it programmed — instant attack, no sustain, a long decay. Only the waveshape is ours, and it is a sawtooth because $D404 says $21.

    And then there is a fourth stream. Two hundred and sixteen bytes at $64BA, in exactly the same format, correctly terminated — and nothing in the entire 47K points at it. The two bytes BA 64 do not occur anywhere in the file. It has been sitting between the harmony and the bass since 1984, and no copy of this game has ever played it.

    So we played it. Not by decoding it and pretending — by booting the game, waiting for the music to start, poking the harmony voice’s pointer to $64B8, and letting the game’s own interrupt-driven player run it. Every note it wrote to the sound chip matched the bytes exactly.

    The stream nothing points at

    Fifty-seven seconds, from $64BA, captured the same way: the game playing it on its own hardware, logged and played back.

    If it sounds familiar, that is because it is the last third of the track above. Those 216 bytes are a byte-for-byte duplicate of the last 216 bytes of the harmony voice: $63DA–$64B1, copied to $64BA–$6591, all of them, position for position.

    Which is a better story than a lost tune, and a more honest one. This is not a cut arrangement or a hidden track. It is what happens when somebody duplicates a block in an editor at two in the morning, moves on, and the file gets saved.

    How we know — that it is unreachable, and that it is a copy

    Unreachable. The player reads its position from three pairs of zero-page bytes, and exactly one routine in the program ever writes any of them: $9170, which sets $13/$14 to $5FFE, $15/$16 to $631E and $2B/$2C to $659E — each two below the start of a stream, because the player increments before it reads. Listing every instruction that touches those six addresses returns that routine and the players themselves, and nothing else. As a second check, neither BA 64 nor B8 64 — the orphan’s address, in either the plain or the pre-increment form a stored pointer would take — occurs anywhere in the image.

    A copy. Compare $63DA–$64B1 with $64BA–$6591: 216 bytes, identical at every position. A longest-common-substring search returns the whole thing, not a prefix.

    Really playable. The recording above is a capture of every write the game made to the sound chip after its harmony pointer was moved to the orphan, and the note sequence in that capture matches the bytes at $64BA exactly.

    Type OATS

    Folklore says the cheat in this game is GOATS. Folklore is nearly right.

    At $96D2, inside the interrupt handler, a routine walks a five-byte table at $96F7. The table reads 1A 26 0A 16 0D — the keyboard-matrix codes for G O A T S. It reads that table twice at a one-byte offset: one entry is the key you have already pressed and are still holding down, the next is the one it wants.

    The consequence of that offset is that the very first comparison — the one at counter zero — is testing the G entry as a still-held check, not as the key it is waiting for. What actually advances the counter from zero is O. So typing GOATS works, because the G is silently swallowed; and typing OATS works just as well. Somebody baked their own joke into a table, and the first letter of it turned out to be decorative.

    Get to five, and the routine stores a non-zero value in $5E and falls through into the routine that clears the message line. Which means that clearing the message line now puts this straight back:

    And then, as far as anyone has been able to make it behave, almost nothing happens.

    Five places in the program read $5E, and between them they do very little. One draws that banner. One is the attract-mode caption cycler, which returns immediately when the flag is set, so the banner stays up instead of being overwritten. There are no extra lives, no invulnerability, no shield.

    The fifth is the interesting one, and it does not work. In the creature-spawn path at $9751, if cheat mode is on and a key is being held at that instant, the raw key code is stored into $46 — and $46 is the byte the camel routine tests at $9468 to decide whether to jump into the zone-transition code. On paper that is a skip-a-zone cheat.

    We got the first half to fire: boot the game, start a zone, hold the cheat flag and a key code across a couple of seconds of real play, and $46 comes back holding the key. We could not get the second half to do anything. Across five hundred further frames the zone index never moved and the screen never changed zone.

    So the honest state of it is: you type a secret word, the machine tells you that you are cheating, and there is a mechanism behind it that we watched fire and could not make matter.

    The cheat that was never born

    There is a second one, and it is broken in a way you can see at a glance:

    C000  AD 01 DC   LDA $DC01      ; read the keyboard directly
C003  C9 50      CMP #$50
C005  F0 0B      BEQ $C012      ; → start normally
C007  C9 50      CMP #$50       ; ← the same test, again
C009  F0 03      BEQ $C00E
C00B  4C AF 94   JMP $94AF

C00E  A9 29      LDA #$29       ; 41 …
C010  85 58      STA $58        ; … into the zone index

    Nothing between the two comparisons changes the accumulator. The second one can only be reached when the first has already failed, and it tests the identical condition — so it can never be true. It is dead by construction, not by later deletion.

    Had it fired, it would have set the zone index to 41: the forty-second and last zone, REVENGE OF THE MUTANT MUTANT CAMELIDS. Somebody wrote a start-at-the-final-zone cheat, and either never filled in the second key code or broke it in a later edit. It shipped like that.

    The random numbers are Microsoft BASIC

    This is the best thing in the file, and it takes three steps.

    One. The random number generator is four instructions:

    8D1D  E6 24      INC $24
8D1F  A6 24      LDX $24
8D21  BD 00 A0   LDA $A000,X
8D24  60         RTS

    Eleven routines call it. It increments a counter, uses it as an index, and reads a byte from $A000. There is nothing random about it at all — it is a walk through 256 fixed bytes.

    Two. What is at $A000? In the shipped image, eight kilobytes of zero. But the program never writes to $00 or $01 — not one instruction in the whole 47K touches the 6510’s bank-switching port — so the processor keeps its power-on configuration, and at power-on $A000 is BASIC ROM. The game is reading Commodore’s BASIC interpreter as a source of entropy.

    Three. The index is a single byte, so it can only ever reach the first page: $A000–$A0FF. That page holds BASIC’s cold-start vectors, its two dispatch tables, and, from $A09E, the keyword list itself. In plain text:

    <CBMBASIC0> … ENDFORNEXTDATAINPUT#INPUTDIMREADLET
GOTORUNIFRESTOREGOSUBRETURNREMSTOPONWAIT
LOADSAVEVERIFYDEFPOKEPR

    The randomness in Revenge of the Mutant Camels is the spelling of the BASIC keywords.

    That would be a curiosity on its own. It matters because of what one of those eleven callers does with it.

    Ten zones almost nobody saw

    The title screen offers two modes, chosen with the function keys: normal, which runs the zones in order, and random, which the credits describe like this:

    OR RANDOM WAVE SEQUENCY, WHERE YOUR NEXT WAVE IS RANDOMLY DRAWN FROM ANY OF THE FIRST 32.

    Which is exactly, literally true. Press F1 and a flag at $59 is set; from then on, choosing the next zone runs this:

    9383  A5 59      LDA $59        ; random mode?
9385  F0 07      BEQ $938E
9387  20 1D 8D   JSR $8D1D      ; a byte of BASIC ROM
938A  29 1F      AND #$1F       ; keep five bits → 0..31
938C  85 58      STA $58        ; that is your next zone

    Five bits. Zones 33 to 42 are structurally unreachable in random mode. All ten of them — including Pac It In, Zone Gunner, Hi Fi Hassles, Zapstars III: Geometrica, Beastly Bonanza and Revenge of the Mutant Mutant Camelids — are seen only by somebody who plays the whole game in order. They are the faded ones in the list above.

    And because the byte comes from a fixed 256-byte page, the odds are not merely biased — they are computable, exactly, and identical on every Commodore 64 ever made. Here is how often each zone comes up, across the whole page:

    This Kiosk Is A Nuclear Free Zone is the most likely wave in the game, at sixteen chances in 256. Several Sinister Space Ships is the least, at two. Not because anyone decided that, but because of how many bytes whose low five bits are 00101 happen to fall in the first page of Microsoft BASIC.

    How we know — that nothing re-rolls it

    Thirteen instructions in the program write $58 directly. They are: the initialisation to zero at boot, the ordinary sequential advance at $9D59, the dead cheat at $C010, and this one. Every instruction between $938C — where the masked byte is stored — and $93E0, where the zone pointer is computed from it, was read: a digit-display update and eight calls, none of which touch $58. Nothing clamps it, and nothing re-rolls it.

    Things left lying about

    Four of them, and together they say what kind of file this is.

    The sprite bank that is there twice

    Two kilobytes at $0801 are byte-for-byte identical to the two kilobytes at $1001. Not zeros, not padding: real artwork — the helicopters, the parachutists, the Space Invaders, the airliner — present twice.

    That is the shape a double-buffered sprite bank would have, which is suggestive — because this game does contain a half-finished sprite multiplexer.

    The multiplexer that only ever runs one half

    At $925F there is a parity flag — INC $30 / AND #$01 / STA $30 — and two nearly identical drawing routines, one for each parity, reading from two side-by-side arrays of object fields. Sixteen conceptual object slots, eight real hardware sprites, one half drawn per frame: a textbook multiplexer, wired up and running.

    Except that the routine which allocates an object slot is bounded by that per-zone +$9B byte, which is 8 in forty-one zones and 6 in one. Nothing can ever allocate above slot 7. The second half of the mechanism runs faithfully, every other frame, over fields that nothing populates.

    How firm this one is

    Firmer than “probably”, softer than the rest of this article, and worth saying so.

    The second field array has no directly-addressed writer anywhere in the program. Watching those addresses during real gameplay — nine hundred frames with the fire button down — produced exactly one write, at the very first byte, from a loop whose index tops out one past the end of the first array. That is a fencepost overlap, not a second population.

    What cannot be ruled out: writes through a pointer. Seventeen indirect accesses near this code cannot be resolved statically, and one of them could in principle reach these fields. So: no direct writer, no observed writes in play, and a slot allocator that structurally cannot reach those slots — but not a proof.

    The routine that cannot be called

    At $C023 a routine pokes seven instruction bytes into seven different places in the running program, turning LDA into DEC, LDA into STA, LDA into INC. It is one half of a toggle: a matching routine at $C046 pokes them all back.

    Two facts about that second routine. First, nothing calls it. No instruction refers to $C046, and the two bytes 46 C0 — its own address, as any pointer or pushed return would have to store it — do not occur anywhere in the 47,390 bytes. It is unreachable by any route the machine has.

    Second, and better: all seven target bytes in the shipped file already hold the poked values. Not one still shows its original form. The toggle can only ever run forwards, and the file was saved with it already applied.

    The high-score file is named after the wrong game

    At $C065 the program opens a file on drive 8 and loads it. The filename lives at $C100 and reads @:ATTACK MUTANT.HI.

    Attack, not Revenge. Attack of the Mutant Camels is the previous game. Either this build inherited the earlier game’s score file wholesale, or a name was copied and never changed — and either way it is the sort of thing a shipped product carries because nobody looked.

    The proof that this is a memory dump

    Everything above hints at it. Two things settle it.

    The high-score table had already been initialised. The game ships four default high scores, and they are jokes:

    1. I LIKE CAMELS REALLY
    2. I GOT NOTHING AGAINST SHEEP EITHER
    3. LLAMAS ARE LLOVELY
    4. 2D SPACE INVADERS RULE THE ZONE OK

    They exist twice in the file. At $5474 there is a 208-byte block in ordinary ASCII — the master. At $5E00 there is a 208-byte block in screen codes — the live copy. Every one of the 208 bytes satisfies master AND $3F = live; 119 are identical and 89 differ by exactly that mask, and none differs any other way. Which is precisely what the game’s own start-up routine does to them.

    The routine had already run when the image was saved.

    And the author’s source code is still in there. Sitting in the middle of the data, at $5870 and a couple of other places, are blocks of readable 6502 assembler stored the way an in-BASIC assembler keeps its source buffer: a link pointer, a line number, the text, a zero. The links resolve, and the line numbers ascend in tens.

    15150   CLC
15160   ADC #$C8
15170   STA NEXINI
15180   LDA NEXINI+1
15190   ADC #$00

15240  MLOOP JSR STARF
15250        JSR BULITZ
15260        JSR CCAMEL

    The first fragment is the loop that walks the zone table, in the author’s own hand: add two hundred, store it in something he called NEXINI. It is the same ADC #$C8 the game executes at $93E4, which is how a table of 200-byte records got established twice over — once from the machine code, once from the source that produced it.

    The second is the main loop, and the names land on real addresses: STARF is the starfield at $8FB0, BULITZ is the bullet at $95B9, CCAMEL is you, at $9444. A third fragment matches the code at $92F6 instruction for instruction, which is how we know these scraps are from this build rather than something older that happened to be lying around: the assembler had the source in memory, the assembled program was in memory next to it, and the whole of memory was written to a disk and sold.

    There is even a comment in there. One of the lines reads ; READ DATA TABLE, and another, further up, just says KEY RESTARTS.

    What it adds up to

    None of this is a criticism. In 1984 you shipped what was in the machine, because the machine was the development environment and there was no build step to be clean about. What went in the box was a photograph of a working session, complete with the things on the desk that were not meant to be in the picture: a duplicated block of music, a spare set of sprites, a cheat somebody broke and never noticed, a toggle stuck in the on position, and a source listing.

    And forty-two names, each centred by hand in a forty-character field, for a game about a camel.

    Careful with that axe, Eugene.

    How this was made. The game was decrunched by running it, then read and photographed with re64, an experimental disassembler in which a person and two AI readers share one live document. Every address here is an address in the 47,390-byte runtime image, and every claim was either derived from that image directly or checked against a scenario that runs on an emulated 6510.

    The pictures. Every screenshot is a single video frame from a real run, characters and hardware sprites alike, exactly as the chip composed it. The sprite and character plates — the menagerie, the camel walk, the font grid, the creature chains — are different: those are drawn straight out of the file at one pixel per pixel, mostly in a single colour, because what colour and what size a sprite gets are decided by the zone it appears in rather than by the picture itself.

    The sound. Both recordings are made from logs of what the program wrote to the sound chip while it ran, with cycle timestamps — pitches from the frequency registers, note lengths from the gate bits, envelope from the ADSR registers. What is reconstructed is the waveshape and the exact curve of the decay, because we are not emulating a SID; what is measured is every note and every duration. The unreachable stream was played by pointing the game’s own player at it and letting it run.
